input.strategy_title: AMD GPU (ROCm) enablement for serving and training
input.strategy_markdown:
## Problem Statement

Two strategic customers are standardizing on AMD Instinct accelerators and need
RHOAI to serve and train on ROCm. Upstream vLLM and PyTorch both publish ROCm
support, but the platform ships only CUDA runtime builds, and we have no
first-hand data on functional or performance parity for our supported model
set. Feature and performance validation requires physical AMD GPU hardware —
none exists in our CI fleet today — and upstream ROCm image cadence is
controlled by AMD and the upstream communities.

## High-Level Requirements

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| HLR-1 | P0 | A validation campaign on physical AMD Instinct hardware establishes functional and performance parity data for vLLM serving of the supported model set, producing the go/no-go scope for productization. |
| HLR-2 | P0 | A supported vLLM ROCm serving runtime is productized for the models the validation campaign clears. |
| HLR-3 | P1 | PyTorch training on ROCm is supported for single- and multi-GPU jobs admitted through Kueue, with amd.com/gpu quota handling. |
| HLR-4 | P2 | Documentation states supported AMD hardware, driver prerequisites, and the validated model list. |

## Affected Components

- KServe
- Serving Runtimes
- Training Operator
- Distributed Workloads

## Out of Scope

- Intel Gaudi or other non-AMD accelerator families
- AMD GPU sharing/partitioning support

## Open Questions

1. Hardware access: the validation campaign (HLR-1) needs dedicated AMD
   Instinct nodes — procurement or partner-lab access is unresolved.
2. Upstream ROCm build cadence: whether AMD's runtime image releases align
   with our release trains is outside our control.

# AMD Instinct validation campaign for vLLM ROCm serving parity

## Description

This epic runs a validation campaign on physical AMD Instinct accelerator hardware to establish functional and performance parity data for vLLM serving of the platform's supported model set, and produces the go/no-go scope that determines which models are productized for ROCm serving. It resolves the central unknown of the AMD enablement strategy: whether upstream vLLM ROCm builds deliver acceptable functional correctness and performance for the models the platform supports, measured first-hand rather than assumed from upstream claims.

## Scope

- Define the validation matrix: the supported model set to be tested, functional pass/fail criteria per model (correct outputs against the CUDA baseline behavior), and performance parity comparison targets versus the productized CUDA builds.
- Secure access to dedicated AMD Instinct nodes (procurement or partner-lab access — see Risks); stand up the test environment with the required ROCm driver level.
- Execute the functional validation runs of vLLM ROCm serving builds for each model in the matrix on the physical hardware.
- Execute the performance benchmark runs and collect parity data (throughput, latency) against the CUDA baseline for the same models and serving configurations.
- Produce the validation report: per-model functional results, performance parity data, and the go/no-go recommendation with the cleared model list for productization.
- Produce the go/no-go scope document that downstream productization work builds against.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The validation matrix (model set, functional pass/fail criteria, performance parity baselines) is documented and reviewed before campaign execution begins.
- Functional validation results exist for every model in the validated matrix, each recorded as pass or fail against the defined criteria.
- Performance parity data is collected for the models that pass functional validation, with the serving configuration and hardware specification recorded alongside the measurements.
- The validation report states, for each model in the matrix, whether it is cleared for productization, and the report is delivered.
- The go/no-go scope for productization is published, enumerating the cleared model list (which may be empty or partial) with the supporting data.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0): A validation campaign on physical AMD Instinct hardware establishes functional and performance parity data for vLLM serving of the supported model set, producing the go/no-go scope for productization.

## Risks

- Hardware access is an external availability precondition: dedicated AMD Instinct nodes do not exist in the CI fleet, and procurement or partner-lab access is unresolved (strategy open question 1). The epic's work includes securing access, but the grant itself is outside the strategy's control and may delay campaign start; the acceptance criteria sit on the campaign's deliverables, not on the access grant.
- Upstream ROCm image cadence is controlled by AMD and the upstream communities; the campaign tests against the image versions available at execution time.

## Notes

- The campaign outcome gates the productization of the vLLM ROCm serving runtime: a partial clear rewrites the productization scope to the cleared model list; a full no-go removes the productization work entirely.

# Productize supported vLLM ROCm serving runtime

## Description

This epic productizes a supported vLLM ROCm serving runtime for the models cleared by the AMD Instinct validation campaign, making ROCm an officially supported accelerator option for model serving alongside the existing CUDA builds. It builds the ROCm variant of the vLLM runtime image in the existing midstream serving runtimes repo, wires it into the platform's serving runtime support, and validates that it serves through the standard KServe deployment flow on AMD GPU nodes.

## Scope

- Build the vLLM ROCm runtime image variant in the existing midstream vLLM repo, following the same build and release process as the productized CUDA runtime images.
- Pin the upstream ROCm base/runtime image version to one that aligns with the target platform release train, and record the alignment decision.
- Define the supported ServingRuntime configuration for the ROCm vLLM variant covering the cleared model list, including the AMD GPU resource requirements (amd.com/gpu) for accelerator assignment.
- Productize the runtime for exactly the models cleared by the validation campaign's go/no-go scope.
- Validate that the ROCm runtime serves through the standard KServe InferenceService and ServingRuntime flow (KServe itself requires no code changes — this is a validation of the passive component, not a modification of it).
- Ensure the ROCm image build is released through the standard serving runtimes build pipeline.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The vLLM ROCm runtime image builds and is released through the standard serving runtimes build pipeline, with the pipeline green for the release build.
- The pinned upstream ROCm image version and its release-train alignment are documented in the epic's deliverable.
- A ServingRuntime configuration for the ROCm vLLM variant exists and is supported for every model on the cleared list, and no model outside the cleared list is advertised as supported.
- A model from the cleared list is served via a standard KServe InferenceService using the ROCm runtime on AMD GPU nodes, with the InferenceService reaching Ready status and serving inference requests successfully (KServe passive-component validation).
- The supported scope (models, hardware, driver level) is recorded for handoff to documentation.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 (P0): A supported vLLM ROCm serving runtime is productized for the models the validation campaign clears.

## Risks

- Upstream ROCm image release cadence is controlled by AMD and the upstream communities (strategy open question 2); if no upstream image version aligns with the target release train, the pinned version and release timing must be renegotiated. This is an alignment risk on this epic's deliverable, not a gate on starting the work.
- The KServe passive-validation acceptance criterion requires serving on AMD GPU nodes, so it depends on the same unresolved AMD Instinct hardware access as the validation campaign (strategy open question 1): procurement or partner-lab access is not yet granted, which may delay the validation runs even though the image build and ServingRuntime configuration work proceed independently.

## Notes

- The scope of this epic (which models are productized) is determined by the validation campaign's go/no-go outcome: a partial clear narrows the model list; a full no-go removes this epic's work. The campaign's validated report and cleared model list are prerequisites.

# PyTorch ROCm training support with Kueue admission and amd.com/gpu quota

## Description

This epic makes PyTorch training on ROCm a supported capability for single- and multi-GPU jobs admitted through Kueue, including handling of the amd.com/gpu resource in the queueing and quota model. It extends the Distributed Workloads stack's supported accelerator resources beyond NVIDIA GPUs so that PyTorchJobs using PyTorch ROCm runtime images can be queued, admitted with gang semantics, and accounted against amd.com/gpu quota.

## Scope

- Enable amd.com/gpu as a supported quota resource in the Distributed Workloads queueing configuration (ClusterQueue/LocalQueue resource flavors), mirroring the existing NVIDIA GPU quota handling.
- Validate that single-GPU and multi-GPU PyTorchJobs running PyTorch ROCm images are admitted through Kueue with all-or-nothing (gang) semantics on AMD GPU nodes.
- Validate the Training Operator path for ROCm jobs (PyTorchJob CRD with ROCm container images and amd.com/gpu resource requests — the Training Operator itself requires no code changes; this is a validation of the passive component).
- Document the supported job shapes (single- and multi-GPU) and any constraints discovered for multi-node ROCm training.
- Validate quota accounting: jobs consuming amd.com/gpu are charged against the configured quota and queue correctly when quota is exhausted.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A ClusterQueue/LocalQueue configuration supporting amd.com/gpu quota exists and is validated.
- A single-GPU PyTorchJob using a PyTorch ROCm image is admitted through Kueue and runs to completion on an AMD GPU node.
- A multi-GPU PyTorchJob using a PyTorch ROCm image is admitted through Kueue with gang semantics (all pods ready before admission completes) and runs to completion.
- Quota accounting for amd.com/gpu is demonstrated: a job exceeding available quota stays pending and is admitted only when quota is available.
- The supported job shapes and configuration requirements for PyTorch ROCm training are recorded for handoff to documentation.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P1): PyTorch training on ROCm is supported for single- and multi-GPU jobs admitted through Kueue, with amd.com/gpu quota handling.

## Risks

- Validation of the supported job shapes requires access to AMD Instinct nodes; hardware availability (strategy open question 1) may delay the validation runs, though the configuration work proceeds independently.

## Notes

- This epic spans the Distributed Workloads component (quota/admission changes and validation — the epic's assigned component) and the Training Operator component (validation only, no code changes; same owning team).
- Uses upstream PyTorch ROCm images as published; no upstream contribution is required from this strategy.

# Document AMD hardware support, driver prerequisites, and validated model list

## Description

This epic authors the user-facing documentation for AMD GPU (ROCm) enablement: the supported AMD hardware, the driver prerequisites for running ROCm workloads, the validated model list for vLLM ROCm serving, and the supported PyTorch training configuration with amd.com/gpu quota. The documentation describes what was built and validated by the serving productization and training support work.

## Scope

Content outline (topics to be authored within this epic's scope):

- Supported AMD hardware: the supported AMD Instinct accelerator models and node requirements for both serving and training.
- Driver prerequisites: the required ROCm driver levels and installation/verification guidance for cluster administrators.
- Validated model list: the models cleared by the validation campaign and productized for ROCm serving, with any per-model performance notes from the parity data.
- PyTorch training on ROCm: supported job shapes (single- and multi-GPU), Kueue admission with amd.com/gpu quota configuration, and example job specifications.
- Limitations: explicitly state what is not supported (other accelerator families, AMD GPU sharing/partitioning) per the strategy's out-of-scope boundaries.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Documentation topics covering supported AMD hardware, driver prerequisites, the validated model list, and PyTorch ROCm training configuration are authored and published through the Red Hat docs content process.
- The documented model list matches exactly the models cleared for productization by the validation campaign.
- The documented driver prerequisites and hardware requirements match the environment validated during the campaign and productization.
- All documentation is technically reviewed against the implemented productized runtime and training support by the owning engineering teams, with review sign-off recorded.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-4 (P2): Documentation states supported AMD hardware, driver prerequisites, and the validated model list.

## Notes

- Epic priority is P1 per the docs-authoring priority exception (strategy frontmatter `priority: Major`), not the P2 of the underlying HLR.
- Depends on the validation campaign (for the validated model list and hardware data), the serving runtime productization, and the training support work, since the documentation describes their outcomes.
